splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes priority over agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines or criminal statutes.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. This split affects how sentencing enhancements are applied across the federal system, with significant implications for criminal defendants' liberty interests.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity should take priority over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, including Sentencing Guidelines, because deference in favor of the government effectively replaces lenity with a 'doctrine of severity.'

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary interpretations takes priority over the rule of lenity when Guidelines provisions are ambiguous, allowing anti-defendant readings to control.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any single criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief under the First Step Act only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria (conjunctive reading of 'and') or if possessing any one criterion is disqualifying (disjunctive reading). This split leads to dramatically different sentencing outcomes for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on geography.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any single criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or.'

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference when the guideline text itself does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1's expansion of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and attempt is a valid, authoritative interpretation of the guideline text under Stinson/Kisor or instead impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its unambiguous text. This split directly affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify for the career-offender enhancement.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is a permissible interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and that inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as 'controlled substance offenses' for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Application Note 1 exceeds the guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses like conspiracy from the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its plain meaning.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines (U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b)) when the state criminalizes a substance not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires that the underlying substance be federally scheduled. Some circuits read the text broadly to include any state-law drug offense regardless of federal scheduling, while others require a federal-law match. This affects career-offender and other enhanced sentencing determinations.

positions.label: No federal scheduling requirement
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under § 4B1.2(b) broadly includes state-law drug offenses even if the particular substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation.

positions.label: Federal scheduling required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under federal law, requiring a categorical match to the federal schedules.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for an order denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment is governed by the civil filing deadline (60 days when the government is a party) or the criminal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering civil appeal deadlines) or remains part of the criminal case (triggering the shorter criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view holding the civil deadline applies, noting a 'lopsided circuit split.'

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion remains part of the criminal case and the shorter criminal appeal deadline governs.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Manchester Farming Partnership

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute or contribute to an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the extraordinary-and-compelling analysis for compassionate release. Some circuits categorically bar such consideration, while others permit it, especially after the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6). This affects thousands of federal prisoners serving sentences that would be lower under current law.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law may be considered as part of the extraordinary-and-compelling analysis, particularly as recognized by the Sentencing Commission's policy statement at U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging a BOP decision about the conditions or terms of confinement (such as denial of expedited transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring a civil rights action.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must be brought as habeas petitions or may proceed under other civil remedies like Bivens or the APA. This split has 'evolved' over more than half a century and affects which procedural vehicle federal prisoners must use to challenge BOP decisions about earned time credits and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for challenges affecting duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's challenge effectively seeks to alter the duration or terms of physical confinement, including BOP decisions on prerelease custody and earned time credits, habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy.

positions.label: Civil rights or other statutory actions are also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may use civil rights actions or other statutory remedies to challenge conditions of confinement, even when the challenge may affect the duration of custody, as habeas is not the exclusive remedy for all confinement-related claims.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted to Chapter 7 in good faith under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between filing a Chapter 13 petition and converting to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or belongs to the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation belongs to the estate based on the broad scope of § 541(a), while other courts have reached the opposite conclusion. This split affects whether debtors who convert in good faith lose the benefit of property appreciation during the pendency of their case.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A) and the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a), post-petition appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor when converting in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the structure, policies, and legislative history of the Bankruptcy Code.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences for supervised release violations as punishment for the violation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to the purposes of supervised release (facilitating reentry and public safety).
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations at revocation, while other circuits limit revocation sentences to the rehabilitative and reentry purposes of supervised release. This split affects the sentencing framework for hundreds of supervised release revocations each year.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly consider punishment as a purpose of revocation sentencing for supervised release violations, under the authority of United States v. Lewis.

positions.label: Revocation sentences must serve supervised release purposes, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences must be calibrated to the breach of trust and the need to facilitate reentry and protect the public, rather than to punish the defendant for the violation conduct itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: This case addresses whether actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability under ERISA must be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or can be selected afterward. The timing directly affects the amount withdrawing employers must pay, with billions of dollars in potential obligations at stake across thousands of multiemployer plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be established by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuaries may select or update actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing plans to use more current information in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Trustees of IAM National Pension Fund v. M & K Employee Solutions

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects sentencing outcomes for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Fugitive tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled during periods of absconding, meaning the clock stops and the court retains jurisdiction to revoke supervised release beyond the original end date.

positions.label: Fugitive tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory authority for tolling supervised release during absconding, and courts cannot create a common-law doctrine that effectively extends punishment beyond the judicially imposed term.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing successive motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) against raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion, in addition to the requirements of § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, it imposes a stricter gatekeeping standard than Congress may have intended for federal prisoners.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, in addition to the requirements of § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures like mail-in ballot counting deadlines. The split affects whether election administration rules can be challenged before an election or must wait until post-election disputes, with significant implications for voting access and election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when challenging state election laws that allegedly dilute or disadvantage their votes.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized interest in election rules does not constitute a concrete, particularized injury sufficient for Article III standing to challenge state election procedures pre-election.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits disagreed on the standards for evaluating discrimination claims against business operators, including issues of liability and available remedies. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach, indicating a potential circuit split on the applicable legal framework for fair treatment in hospitality, retail, and service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that business operators face broader liability for discrimination claims, with more expansive remedies available to aggrieved customers.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards apply to discrimination claims against business operators, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
